newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Palestinian brokerage houses flooded with business. [CORRECTED 16:00 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Palestinian brokerage houses flooded with business. [CORRECTED 16:00 GMT]

text.p: Businessmen flooded Palestinian brokerage houses on Wednesday with inquiries on investing in the first Palestinian stock market in the West Bank, a day after it opened for limited trading, traders said.

Jamal Aladdin, general manager of the Jordan and Palestine Financial Investment Company, said investors from Jordan and Israel as well as several prominent West Bank Palestinian businessmen visited his firm or phoned to inquire about investment prospects.
"Since last night, we have been getting many calls from local Palestinian investors as well as from Jordan and from Israel inquiring on the possibility for investing," Aladdin told Reuters.

Traders said the interest was partly motivated out of eagerness on the part of expatriate Palestinians to participate in building the economy of the West Bank and Gaza Strip and partly out of pure business interests.
"The inquiries bode very well for the success of the exchange, especially in view of the calls from outside our homeland," Aladdin said.

The Palestine Securities Exchange (PSE) opened for limited trading in the town of Nablus on Tuesday, where several transactions took place. Officials said the exchange, which had listed 23 companies, would start with one trading session per week until trading volume builds up.

"All the signs point to a positive start," said Jiries Qassis, general manager of the Ramallah-based United Securities Company. "Everybody is eager to see an organised market that would provide real values for the shares."

Four brokerage firms were accredited to the exchange, a fully-electronic market which founders say was designed to attract foreign capital and provide an alternative to common forms of investment such as bank deposits and real estate.
Traders said top investors in the Jordanian stock exchange as well as some brokerage firms have also expressed interest in the Palestinian bourse.
Hamaidi al-Barghouthi, a major investor on the Amman stock exchange, praised the management of the PSE and predicted success for the venture.
"I am confident that the exchange will be the best one in the whole Middle East. It has come at the right time," Barghouthi told Reuters.
Qassis said (corrects attribution) he expected more than 100 accounts to be opened with his firm during the first week and that many callers had already expressed interest in trading.

Qassis said he was encouraged by the Palestinian finance minister's comments on Tuesday that the Palestinian Authority plans to make it compulsory for joint-stock companies to list on the stock exchange.
Israel's mass-circulating Yedioth Ahoronoth, in an editorial, welcomed the opening of the exchange as an "important economic event".

"The Nablus stock exchange is doubly symbolic: a symbol of Palestinian economic autonomy and a symbol of an economic and social regime based upon private ownership, free enterprise and market forces," the newspaper said.
